title: Reply: internal inspiration is a stronger writing mandate than vocal order
source_text: XI. Respondeo, verum est Apostolos non fuisse aggressuros summam Evangelicae doctrinae scripto complecti, scriptaque sua Ecclesiae tradere, tanquam fidei normam & regulam, nisi ex divino mandato: Sed eos nullum tale mandatum habuisse falsum est. Id ex Augustino poterant adversarii discere. Nam Augustini verba sunt lib. 1. de consensu Evangelistarum cap. ult. Quicquid Christus de suis dictis & factis nos legere voluit, hoc scribendum Apostolis tanquam suis manibus imperavit. Fieri quidem potest, ut Christus viva voce & expressis verbis istud non praeceperit: Sed dubium esse non potest, nec negare audent ipsi Pontificii, quin ad hoc fuerint a Deo inspirati, & a Spiritu sancto moti extra ordinem. Quod enim Petrus dicit de scriptis propheticis, non voluntate humana allatam olim prophetiam, sed actos fuisse a Spiritu sancto sanctos Dei homines, non minus verum est de scriptis Novi Testamenti. Atque, ut docet Apostolus 2. Tim. 3. Omnis Scriptura, seu Veteris, seu Novi Testamenti, divinitus inspirata est. Itaque Apostoli forte non habuerint externum & vocale scribendi mandatum: At certe mandatum internum habuerunt, eoque fuerunt adducti extraordinario quodam impulsu Spiritus divini, quod est omni mandato fortius. Nec video, ubi constat de divina inspiratione, cur praeterea mandatum externum requiratur.
pass_a_gloss: I answer: it is true the Apostles would not have undertaken to embrace the sum of Evangelical doctrine in writing, and to hand their writings to the Church as the norm and rule of faith, except by divine mandate: But that they had no such mandate is false. Opponents could learn that from Augustine. For Augustine's words are, On the Harmony of the Evangelists book 1, last chapter: Whatever Christ willed us to read of his sayings and deeds, he commanded the Apostles to write as if with his own hands. It may be that Christ did not command this by living voice and express words: But it cannot be doubted — and the Pontiffs themselves dare not deny — that they were inspired by God for this and moved extraordinarily by the Holy Spirit. For what Peter says of the prophetic writings — that prophecy was not formerly brought by human will, but holy men of God were moved by the Holy Spirit — is no less true of the New Testament writings. And as the Apostle teaches in 2 Timothy 3, All Scripture, whether of Old or New Testament, is inspired by God. So the Apostles may not have had an external and vocal mandate to write: Yet they certainly had an internal mandate, and were led by an extraordinary impulse of the divine Spirit, which is stronger than every mandate. Nor do I see, where divine inspiration is established, why an external mandate should still be required.
pass_b_english: Agreed: they would not make writings the rule of faith without a divine mandate.
Denied: that they lacked one — Augustine says Christ ordered the Apostles to write what we should read.
Even without a spoken 'Write!', inspiration and the Spirit's extraordinary impulse are the stronger command.
2 Tim. 3: all Scripture is God-breathed — once that stands, a further vocal warrant is needless.
